profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between two workstreams supporting an international PV performance-loss-rate benchmarking effort under a cross-institution collaboration. One workstream is preparing the shared benchmark package of plant datasets and metadata; the other is consolidating contributed analysis outputs into a comparison table for the next Task 13 subgroup review. The immediate context is that eight participating institutions have already received the current dataset bundle, and the team now needs to align on what will be re-issued before the next review call. The agenda is to confirm which benchmark package is the 'current' one, what quality grading and filtering notes will accompany it, how contributors should format their returned results, and who updates the shared benchmark tracker. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on the dataset handoff, submission expectations, and ownership of the comparison workbook before results are collected.

members.name: Dr. Elena Marquez
members.expertise: PV performance analytics, cross-site dataset curation, metadata harmonization
members.background: Elena works at a European solar R&D institute and coordinates incoming plant and weather datasets from partner labs for collaborative benchmarking exercises.
members.private_state: She wants to minimize churn for external contributors, avoid another full data resend, and keep the benchmark package stable enough that institutions can submit by the review deadline.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to the 'benchmark package,' they mean the March package with only metadata-sheet edits since the raw time-series files were frozen.
A 'cleaned dataset' already excludes flagged outages and sensor faults because pre-cleaning by the data workstream is part of the package, not something analysts redo from scratch.
If contributors are asked for 'uncertainty,' a single headline uncertainty figure per site-method result is sufficient for the comparison workbook.
The shared comparison workbook is owned by the coordination side, so analysts append results there but do not restructure tabs or add method-specific sheets.

members.name: Samuel Okoye
members.expertise: Statistical degradation modeling, reproducible analysis pipelines, benchmark result synthesis
members.background: Samuel works at a university-affiliated energy systems lab and is responsible for consolidating methodological outputs from different institutions into a comparable benchmarking summary.
members.private_state: He wants submissions to be analytically reproducible, rich enough to support method-comparison later, and structured so his team does not have to chase people for missing intermediate assumptions.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the 'benchmark package,' they mean the latest analyst-ready release, including revised exclusion masks and the April tracker notes circulated in the methods subgroup.
A 'cleaned dataset' means quality-graded raw inputs plus flags, after which each analyst applies the agreed filtering logic within their own pipeline.

If contributors are asked for 'uncertainty,' they should provide standard error and confidence interval fields, not just one summary number, because later comparison depends on separating these quantities.
The shared comparison workbook is a living integration artifact managed by the methods side, so adding columns, tabs, and structured method notes is expected.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the current benchmark package' and 'the version everyone already has.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the March package distributed to all eight institutions, with raw files unchanged and only minor metadata clarifications.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the analyst-ready April release used in the methods subgroup, which includes revised exclusion masks and tracker annotations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both packages are evolutions of the same named bundle, and both participants know a recent update happened; because they are discussing continuity rather than re-scoping the study, the phrase sounds specific enough and neither expects that they are indexing different releases.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that contributors should 'use the cleaned dataset' before applying their methods.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'cleaned' means the data package already has outage periods and obvious sensor issues removed, so analysts start from pre-cleaned inputs and then do only method-specific filtering.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'cleaned' means the package contains raw-but-quality-graded data plus flags, and analysts must implement the agreed exclusions themselves within their pipelines.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In benchmarking contexts, 'cleaning' is routinely contrasted with later filtering, but the exact boundary between package-level cleaning and analyst-level filtering is often institutional habit; since both expect some preprocessing to exist, the phrase feels unambiguous enough to pass without challenge.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say each team should return 'the loss rate with uncertainty' for each site.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this means one uncertainty value attached to each reported loss-rate estimate, sufficient for the comparison table and summary slides.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this means a submission must include separate uncertainty-related fields such as standard error and confidence interval bounds, because that is what makes the result complete for downstream method comparison.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are aligned on the high-level goal of capturing uncertainty, and the phrase appears standard in technical reporting; the divergence concerns what counts as an adequate instantiation of that standard, which usually stays implicit unless someone is designing the template line by line.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss 'updating the shared benchmark tracker' after submissions come in.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes the coordination team owns the workbook structure and others only fill designated cells or send her content to enter.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes the methods team is expected to extend and annotate the tracker directly as needed for integration.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Shared workbooks in collaborations often evolve organically, and both participants are accustomed to being responsible in adjacent ways; because no one is resisting the work itself, the hidden assumption about edit rights and structural ownership remains invisible.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to stay simple. Everyone already has the March benchmark package, and I do not want to trigger another round of file transfers just because we clarified a few metadata points. If we can agree on a compact submission format and keep the shared benchmark tracker in its usual structure, partners can still hit the review deadline without churn.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Samuel. I think we just need to align on the current benchmark package, the submission format, and how we're updating the shared benchmark tracker before the next Task 13 review.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that is exactly what matters. As long as everyone is working from the current benchmark package—the analyst-ready one we've been using in the methods subgroup—the integration should be manageable. What I really want is to avoid getting a mix of results based on different exclusion assumptions.
turns.utterance: Yes, that sounds right. If everyone uses the current benchmark package, consolidation on our side should stay pretty straightforward.

turns.inner_thought: I'll keep this focused on notes only. The raw time-series files were frozen in March, and the last thing I need is eight institutions thinking they have to download everything again. A metadata note resend is enough.
turns.utterance: Since everyone already has the package, my plan was to resend only the revised metadata notes rather than pushing the files again.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine if the notes preserve the latest package basis, especially the revised exclusion masks and tracker annotations we've been relying on. I don't need another bulky distribution, but I do need analysts to use the same exclusion basis when they build their pipelines from the cleaned dataset.
turns.utterance: That works for me, as long as the revised exclusion notes tied to the latest package remain the basis for analysis.

turns.inner_thought: Right, contributors should begin from the cleaned dataset we've already prepared, with outages and obvious sensor faults already handled at package level. Then they can do their own method-specific steps without reopening basic data cleaning.
turns.utterance: Exactly. My view is that contributors should use the cleaned dataset before applying their methods, so the benchmark stays comparable.

turns.inner_thought: Yes—use the cleaned dataset in the sense of starting from the quality-graded inputs and then implementing the agreed cleaning and filtering logic inside each reproducible pipeline. If they document exclusions, we'll be able to compare approaches later without guessing what they did.
turns.utterance: Agreed. Analysts can use the cleaned dataset and implement the cleaning and filtering steps in their own pipelines, as long as they document what they excluded.

turns.inner_thought: I want the return template lean: one row per site-method result in the workbook, with the loss rate and uncertainty included. A single uncertainty value is enough for the comparison table and the review slides; anything more detailed can become a coordination headache.
turns.utterance: On submissions, I'd suggest each team return one row per site-method combination with the loss rate and uncertainty for each site, so the comparison table stays compact.

turns.inner_thought: That is fine structurally, provided the submission still carries the uncertainty components we need downstream. If they include standard error and confidence interval information in the same row set, my team won't have to chase missing fields later.
turns.utterance: That format works. They can include the standard error and confidence interval in the same submission as well, so nothing gets lost later.

turns.inner_thought: I'll keep control of the workbook structure. The coordination side owns that shared benchmark tracker, and I don't want tabs multiplying right before the deadline. Teams should just populate the usual fields and leave the layout intact.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll keep the shared benchmark tracker tidy, and once results are ready, teams can populate the usual fields there.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect—then my group can work directly in the tracker during integration. We will likely need to add method notes and probably a couple of extra tabs for synthesis, which is normal if the tracker is serving as the living integration artifact.
turns.utterance: Sure, and my group can update the shared benchmark tracker directly with method notes and any extra tabs we need during result integration.

turns.inner_thought: This seems settled. I'll send a concise note pointing partners back to the current benchmark package as they already know it, remind them not to wait for a new file drop, and ask for the loss rate with uncertainty by the review deadline.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll circulate notes after this and remind partners to work from the current package and submit by the review deadline.

turns.inner_thought: Good. Once the tracker starts getting updated and the site submissions come in, we can consolidate quickly—assuming people include the uncertainty details and method notes we need. This should put us in good shape for the subgroup review.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll be ready to consolidate the incoming results once the tracker updates and site submissions start arriving.
